```{python}
#| label: setup
import os, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
# MVBBSC (the live B-MV row) draws 4 NUTS chains via NumPyro; give JAX four host
# devices so they run in parallel on a single-CPU renderer (set before any JAX import).
os.environ.setdefault("JAX_PLATFORM_NAME", "cpu")
os.environ.setdefault("XLA_FLAGS", "--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=4")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import Markdown

def _find_up(name, start, hops=6):
    d = os.path.abspath(start)
    for _ in range(hops):
        if os.path.exists(os.path.join(d, name)):
            return d
        d = os.path.dirname(d)
    return os.path.abspath(start)

ROOT = _find_up("basedata", os.getcwd())
BASE = os.path.join(ROOT, "basedata")
DATA = os.getcwd() if os.path.exists(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "data", "basc_weights.csv")) \
    else os.path.join(ROOT, "review", "basc_westgermany")
DATA = os.path.join(DATA, "data")
```

## The question

The authors write in their responses "*we have removed the normalization step and re-run the entire West Germany analysis using the original per-capita GDP scale, consistent with the standard setup of Abadie et al. (2010, 2015). Accordingly, the description of the normalization procedure has been removed from Section 5, and all empirical results have been updated, including the posterior donor inclusion probabilities, donor weights, counterfactual trajectories, credible intervals, and the estimated treatment effects. The revised results lead to the same substantive conclusions as those reported in the previous version.*" By this, I take them to mean "we took the original West Germany data (that was un-transformed) and ran SCM, BASC, and the others through this exact dataset." It is against this claim that I view the second round of review.

On the BASC side that claim checks out. The authors' public sampler (`BASC_realdata.R` at `github.com/sll-lee/paper-BASC`) prepares the outcome as `y <- raw.y` and the donor matrix as `x <- t(raw.x)`, commented "Final manuscript version: original per-capita GDP scale". The pre-1990 mean and standard deviation are still computed there but no longer applied. Running that sampler myself, on much shorter chains than the paper's, returns a post-1990 ATT in the range -390 to -702 against the paper's reported -434, and selects the same three donors the paper's own Table 7 does. So BASC itself is on the scale the authors say, and it reproduces.

The difficulty is with the four methods BASC is compared against, none of which appear in that repository at all.


BASC is presented as a competitive-or-superior synthetic-control estimator, and Section 5 is offered as the empirical evidence for that. My objection is not that BASC fits the pre-1990 path less well than the alternatives and is therefore the inferior method; in-sample fit is one criterion among several, and the Bottom line below sets out why I do not treat it as decisive on its own. The objection is narrower and, I think, harder to answer: on the canonical application, BASC fits far worse than the methods it extends and competes with, while two of the comparison results it is measured against are themselves inconsistent with the estimators the paper says produced them. The application therefore cannot presently establish the competitiveness it is offered to establish.

Two findings carry that, and neither depends on an estimator of mine. The first is that BASC estimates its donor weights from the post-treatment outcomes. Equation (7) is written over $t = 1,\dots,T$, and the likelihood scores residuals across all 44 years with a single constant absorbing the post-1990 divergence. Constrained least squares under that specification reproduces the paper's published Table 7 weight column to an L1 distance of 0.04, with no sampler, prior or Gaussian process involved, and it accounts for the pre-treatment fit gap that first drew my attention. The second is the s-SCM weight vector printed in the same table, which fails an arithmetic check against the authors' own donor data: multiply the published weights by the published donor series and read off the contradiction. The first is established in the fit section immediately below, the second in the section on Table 7 that follows it.

Below I compare BASC's in-sample (pre-1990) fit on West Germany against `mlsynth`'s own estimators on the identical data (the Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller 2015 `repgermany` panel, original per-capita GDP scale), assembled with `mlsynth`'s `compare_estimators` utility. The `mlsynth` analyses run at render time; BASC is precomputed (its Gibbs sampler runs from the authors' R, `github.com/sll-lee/paper-BASC`).

## Specifications

Standard SCM (s-SCM, per the paper) is run from `mlsynth` in two ways. The first is outcome-only, matching the pre-1990 GDP path. The second uses covariates, in the canonical Abadie et al. (2015) predictor set:

- GDP per capita, inflation rate, trade openness, industry share, averaged 1981–1990;
- investment rate and schooling, averaged 1980–1985.

We estimate the fit via two bilevel solvers: `backend="malo"` and `backend="mscmt"` (MSCMT's nested differential-evolution search).

The robust family is `CLUSTERSC`. Its two paths are not estimators I have introduced into the comparison; they are the paper's own two two-stage methods. `method="rpca"` is the functional-PCA screen followed by robust PCA and non-negative least squares that Section 2.4.1 calls fPCA-SYNTH, after Bayani (2021, 2022). `method="PCR"` is the SVD-clustering-plus-principal-component-regression procedure the paper calls ClusterSC, after Rho et al. (2025). Those two rows can therefore be read straight against the paper's own fPCA-SYNTH and ClusterSC columns.

As a benchmark outside the SCM family entirely, we also include `FDID`, the forward-selected difference-in-differences estimator of Li (2024).

```{python}
#| label: compare
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from mlsynth import VanillaSC, CLUSTERSC, FDID, MVBBSC, compare_estimators

# --- ADH 2015 West Germany covariate specification ---
COVS = ["gdp_avg", "infrate", "trade", "industry", "schooling", "invest80"]
WINDOWS = {"gdp_avg": (1981, 1990), "infrate": (1981, 1990), "trade": (1981, 1990),
           "industry": (1981, 1990), "schooling": (1980, 1985), "invest80": (1980, 1985)}
FIT_WINDOW = (1960, 1989)          # outcome-matching (pre-treatment) window

raw = pd.read_stata(os.path.join(BASE, "repgermany.dta"))
d = raw[["country", "year", "gdp", "infrate", "trade", "industry", "schooling", "invest80"]].copy()
d["gdp_avg"] = d["gdp"]             # GDP per capita as an averaged predictor
d["treat"] = ((d.country == "West Germany") & (d.year >= 1990)).astype(int)

base = dict(df=d, outcome="gdp", treat="treat", unitid="country", time="year",
            display_graphs=False)
cov = dict(covariates=COVS, covariate_windows=WINDOWS, fit_window=FIT_WINDOW, seed=0)

# One panel, several specifications -> compare_estimators does the rest
cmp = compare_estimators({
    "VanillaSC (outcome-only)":    VanillaSC({**base}),
    "VanillaSC (malo, ADH cov)":   VanillaSC({**base, "backend": "malo",  **cov}),
    "VanillaSC (mscmt, ADH cov)":  VanillaSC({**base, "backend": "mscmt", **cov}),
    "CLUSTERSC RPCA-SC (= fPCA-SYNTH)": CLUSTERSC({**base, "method": "rpca", "rpca_method": "PCP"}),
    "CLUSTERSC PCR/RSC (= ClusterSC)":  CLUSTERSC({**base, "method": "PCR"}),
    "FDID (Forward DID)":          FDID({**base}),
    "B-MV (MVBBSC, mlsynth)":   MVBBSC({**base, "n_warmup": 500, "n_samples": 500,
                                           "n_chains": 4, "seed": 0}),
}, show_bands=False)
```


```{python}
#| label: load-basc
basc_cf = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "basc_counterfactual.csv"))        # 2000/2000
basc_cf500 = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "basc_counterfactual_500.csv")) # 500/500
bmv_cf = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "bmv_counterfactual.csv"))          # B-MV via bsynth
```

## In-sample (pre-1990) RMSE by method

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rmse
tbl = (cmp.summary.rename(columns={"pre_rmse": "In-sample RMSE", "att": "ATT"})
       .reset_index().rename(columns={"method": "Method"}))
tbl = tbl[["Method", "In-sample RMSE", "ATT"]]

# BASC in-sample RMSE and post-1990 ATT from each saved posterior counterfactual
# (ATT = mean(observed - synthetic) over 1990+, the same convention as cmp.summary).
def _basc_rmse_att(cf):
    pre, post = cf["year"] < 1990, cf["year"] >= 1990
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((cf.loc[pre, "observed"] - cf.loc[pre, "synthetic"]) ** 2)))
    att = float((cf.loc[post, "observed"] - cf.loc[post, "synthetic"]).mean())
    return rmse, att

rmse_2000, att_2000 = _basc_rmse_att(basc_cf)
rmse_500,  att_500  = _basc_rmse_att(basc_cf500)
# 25000/25000: from the offline chain (seed 200) regenerated by scripts/run_gamma1.R,
# whose control configuration is the authors' sampler unpatched. Its posterior
# counterfactual is not stored or plotted, so the two summary numbers are read from
# the diagnostic table that script writes.
_g25 = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "gamma1_diagnostic.csv")).query("config == 'basc' and N == 25000").iloc[0]
rmse_25k, att_25k = float(_g25.rmse_pre), float(_g25.att_post)
basc_rows = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Method": "BASC (25000 / 25000 MCMC)", "In-sample RMSE": rmse_25k,  "ATT": att_25k},
    {"Method": "BASC (2000 / 2000 MCMC)",   "In-sample RMSE": rmse_2000, "ATT": att_2000},
    {"Method": "BASC (500 / 500 MCMC)",     "In-sample RMSE": rmse_500,  "ATT": att_500},
])
rmse_bmv, att_bmv = _basc_rmse_att(bmv_cf)
bmv_row = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Method": "B-MV (bsynth, Bayesian SCM)", "In-sample RMSE": rmse_bmv, "ATT": att_bmv},
])
full = pd.concat([tbl, bmv_row, basc_rows], ignore_index=True).sort_values("In-sample RMSE").reset_index(drop=True)
Markdown(full.round(1).to_markdown(index=False))
```

Every comparison estimator attains a materially tighter pre-treatment fit than BASC. BASC's pre-1990 RMSE sits in a ~170–195 band across the three chain lengths (burn-in/sampling: 500/500, 2000/2000, 25000/25000), roughly 3 times the plain `VanillaSC` fit (60.8), and about twice the `CLUSTERSC` (88.6 / 98.0) and `FDID` (83.4) fits. Lengthening the MCMC does not close the gap; if anything the best-mixed 25000/25000 chain fits worst.

The most telling row is B-MV, the Bayesian synthetic control of Martinez and Vives-i-Bastida (2024), and it is telling because of the relationship the paper itself establishes between the two models.

Section 3.1 sets out that relationship explicitly. When every donor is selected, so that $\gamma = \mathbf{1}$, the proposed prior on the weights reduces to Equation (11), and the paper states that at $\alpha_u = 1$ this "coincides with the uniform Dirichlet prior in Equation (5), which is used in the implementation of Martinez and Vives-i-Bastida", concluding that the construction "retains the full-simplex Dirichlet construction as a special case". The next sentence introduces the second addition: "we introduce the Gaussian process (GP) term $f_t$ to capture smooth temporal variation in the treated outcome that is not explained by the simplex-constrained donor combination."

So BASC contains B-MV's prior. It is that prior, plus donor selection, plus a nonparametric term whose stated purpose is to absorb precisely the pre-treatment variation the donor combination fails to explain. On this panel the containing model fits the pre-1990 path at 169 to 195 and the contained one at 62.

Instead of speculating about why, I ran the authors' own sampler with $\gamma$ fixed to $\mathbf{1}$. The patch to `BASC_realdata.R` is four lines: the loop that resamples $\gamma_j$ is given an empty index set, and `alpha_u` becomes an argument so that the Section 3.1 configuration ($\alpha_u = 1$) can be run alongside the value the authors actually use. Everything else, the priors, the updates, the Gaussian process, the posterior summary, is their code unmodified. The control confirms it: run without the patch, the sampler returns pre-1990 RMSE 169.4 and ATT -582.5, reproducing the 2000/2000 row of the table above.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-gamma1
g1 = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "gamma1_diagnostic.csv"))
# Greek goes through as math, not as literal Unicode: pdflatex has no glyph for it
_lab = {"basc":    r"as published ($\gamma$ sampled, $\alpha_u = 2.5$)",
        "g1_a2.5": r"$\gamma = 1$, $\alpha_u = 2.5$ (their prior, selection off)",
        "g1_a1":   r"$\gamma = 1$, $\alpha_u = 1$ (the Section 3.1 configuration)"}
_short = g1[g1.N == 2000]
_t = (_short.assign(Configuration=_short.config.map(_lab))
            .pivot_table(index="Configuration", columns="seed", values="rmse_pre", sort=False)
            .round(1))
_t.columns = [f"2000/2000, seed {c}" for c in _t.columns]
_long = g1[g1.N == 25000].set_index(g1[g1.N == 25000].config.map(_lab)).rmse_pre.round(1)
_t["25000/25000"] = _long.reindex(_t.index).values
_t["donors kept"] = _short.groupby(_short.config.map(_lab), sort=False).n_donors.max().values
Markdown("Pre-1990 RMSE from the authors' sampler, burn-in / sampling as shown:\n\n"
         + _t.reset_index().to_markdown(index=False))
```

Donor selection is not what costs the fit. Removing it makes the fit worse, and the Section 3.1 configuration lands at 193 to 196 in every seed and at 195 when the chain is lengthened fiftyfold, not at the 62 the correspondence with B-MV would suggest. Chain length is not the constraint: the control returns 195.5 at 25000/25000 against 169.4 at 2000/2000, so the published configuration fits worse with more sampling, not better. The Gaussian process is inert throughout, its posterior mean path having a standard deviation of about 1 unit against residuals near 200, so the counterfactual is the donor combination alone to two decimal places.

The reason is the likelihood, and the paper states it. Equation (7) is written for $t = 1,\dots,T$: the treated outcome is the simplex-weighted donor combination plus $f_t$ plus $\sum_m \alpha_m D_{mt} I(t > T_0)$ plus noise, over the whole sample. The sampler implements exactly that, and `loglik_gamma` scores `y - x %*% beta - Dt * alpha.v - f` across all 44 years. The donor weights are therefore estimated from the post-treatment outcomes as well as the pre-treatment ones. B-MV conditions on the pre-period, as standard synthetic-control practice does. The Section 3.1 statement is about the prior, and it is correct about the prior; it does not make BASC nest B-MV as an estimator, so the two fits were never going to agree.

Section 3.1 also fixes the shape of the post-treatment term for this comparison. The paper offers polynomial and spline bases for $D_{mt}$, and then sets $q = 1$ with $D_{1t} = 1$ "in the simplest specification used for comparison with standard SCM", so the entire post-1990 divergence is absorbed by one constant over fourteen years. West Germany's gap from any donor combination widens across that window, so a single constant cannot absorb it and the residual is taken up by the weights. The published sampler implements only this case: `Dt * alpha.v` is scalar recycling, which is what raises R's deprecation warning on every iteration, so the flexible effect bases the paper describes are not in the code that produced these results.

This is also where the consistency theorem stops covering the estimator. Theorem 3.3 is proved on $y^-_1 = Y^-_0 w + \epsilon$, restricted to $t = 1,\dots,T_0$, a model the paper says "excludes the Gaussian process term and the post-intervention effect term". That is the pre-period-only specification, which is precisely the one whose weights are not exposed to the post-treatment outcomes. The theorem therefore establishes donor-set consistency for an estimator other than the one fitted in Section 5, and the term it sets aside is the one that produces the behaviour below.

That difference accounts for the numbers on its own, with no MCMC involved. Below, the weights are chosen by constrained least squares under the same simplex constraint, once on the pre-period alone, which is the standard synthetic control, and once on all 44 years with one constant post-treatment shift, which is what BASC's likelihood scores.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-fullsample-ls
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
import cvxpy as cp
from mlsynth.utils.datautils import dataprep

_p = dataprep(d, "country", "year", "gdp", "treat")
_y = np.asarray(_p["y"]).flatten(); _X = np.asarray(_p["donor_matrix"])
_names = list(_p["donor_names"]); _npre = int(_p["pre_periods"])
_pre = np.arange(len(_y)) < _npre; _D = (~_pre).astype(float)

def _solve(mask, free_alpha):
    w = cp.Variable(_X.shape[1], nonneg=True); a = cp.Variable(1)
    r = _y[mask] - _X[mask] @ w - (cp.multiply(_D[mask], a) if free_alpha else 0)
    cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(cp.sum_squares(r)), [cp.sum(w) == 1]).solve(solver=cp.CLARABEL)
    return np.asarray(w.value).ravel(), float(np.atleast_1d(a.value)[0]) if free_alpha else 0.0

w_pre, _   = _solve(_pre, False)
w_all, a_all = _solve(np.ones(len(_y), bool), True)
_rm = lambda w: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((_y[_pre] - (_X @ w)[_pre]) ** 2)))
Markdown(pd.DataFrame({
    "Weights fit on": ["pre-1990 only (standard SCM)", "all 44 years, one constant shift"],
    "pre-1990 RMSE": [round(_rm(w_pre), 1), round(_rm(w_all), 1)],
    "post-1990 effect": [round(float((_y[~_pre] - (_X @ w_pre)[~_pre]).mean()), 0), round(a_all, 0)],
}).to_markdown(index=False))
```

The second row is BASC. Its pre-1990 fit of 198 sits inside the 193 to 206 band the sampler produces, and its constant shift of -351 sits inside the -195 to -582 range of the sampler's ATT. The weights match the paper's published column:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ls-vs-table7
paper_basc = {"USA": 0.00, "UK": 0.00, "Austria": 0.00, "Belgium": 0.00, "Denmark": 0.00,
              "France": 0.00, "Italy": 0.12, "Netherlands": 0.00, "Norway": 0.00,
              "Switzerland": 0.44, "Japan": 0.37, "Greece": 0.01, "Portugal": 0.05,
              "Spain": 0.00, "Australia": 0.00, "New Zealand": 0.00}
_w = pd.DataFrame({"Donor": _names,
                   "BASC, paper Table 7": [paper_basc[n] for n in _names],
                   "Least squares, all 44 years": w_all.round(3)})
_l1 = float(abs(_w.iloc[:, 1] - _w.iloc[:, 2]).sum())
Markdown(_w[_w.iloc[:, 1:].abs().max(axis=1) > 0.005].to_markdown(index=False)
         + f"\n\nDonors below 0.005 in both columns are omitted. L1 distance between the two columns: {_l1:.3f}.")
```

The paper's published BASC donor weights are what constrained least squares returns when the post-treatment outcomes are allowed to inform the weights. No prior, no sampler, no Gaussian process and no donor selection is needed to produce them.

Two consequences follow, and both are for the authors. The pre-treatment fit reported for BASC is not evidence about how well a synthetic West Germany can be constructed, because the weights were not chosen to construct one, and setting it beside the pre-treatment fit of standard SCM compares quantities that were minimised over different periods. And the reported effect is estimated jointly with weights that are themselves fitted to the divergence the effect is meant to measure, which is why the same simplex constraint yields -1,298 when the weights are set on the pre-period and -351 when they are not.

This is not a discrepancy between the paper and the code. Equation (7) specifies the full-sample model, Section 3.1 specifies the constant post-treatment shift, and the sampler implements both faithfully. It is a consequence of a stated design that the paper does not discuss, arising in the one place where the design and the comparison interact most sharply, and it is not covered by the theory the paper offers.

Fitting over the whole sample is not itself the problem. If the post-treatment term can absorb the post-treatment residual exactly, the treated observations after $T_0$ carry no information about $w$ whatever their values, and the weights are determined by the pre-period alone. Under least squares with one free parameter per post-treatment year that is exactly what happens: the estimate returns the pre-period solution to an L1 distance of 0.000, with the same pre-1990 RMSE of 60.8 and the same effect of -1,297. The best case for full-sample fitting is a tie with pre-period fitting. Every more restrictive effect model does worse, because the post-treatment observations then become informative about $w$ through a channel that is the treatment effect itself. What the constant does is force fourteen years of a widening gap through a single parameter, and the residual it cannot take is absorbed by the weights.

That is testable in the authors' own sampler, because Section 3.1 supplies the alternative basis: $D_{1t} = 1$ together with $D_{2t} = t - T_0$. Generalising the released code to accept it is one substitution, `Dt * alpha.v` becoming `Dt %*% alpha.v`, at the five sites where that expression appears, plus a truncated-normal draw valid for a non-diagonal covariance. Run at $q = 1$ the generalised code is bit-identical to the original, returning 166.2, 169.4 and 222.1 across the three seeds and 195.5 at 25000/25000.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-effect-basis
eb = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "effect_basis_diagnostic.csv"))
_l = {"q1_const": r"$q=1$, $D_{1t}=1$ (as published)",
      "q2_linear": r"$q=2$, adding $D_{2t}=t-T_0$"}
_col = lambda r: (f"2000/2000, seed {r.seed}" if r.N == 2000 else "25000/25000")
_p = (eb.assign(Specification=eb.config.map(_l), col=eb.apply(_col, axis=1))
        .pivot_table(index="Specification", columns="col",
                     values=["rmse_pre", "att_post"], sort=False))
_order = [c for c in ["2000/2000, seed 100", "2000/2000, seed 200",
                      "2000/2000, seed 300", "25000/25000"]]
_p = _p.reindex(columns=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([["rmse_pre", "att_post"], _order])).round(0)
_p.columns = [f"{'RMSE' if a == 'rmse_pre' else 'ATT'}, {c}" for a, c in _p.columns]
Markdown(_p.reset_index().to_markdown(index=False))
```

Adding the one term moves the pre-1990 fit from 166 to 222 down to 135 to 149, and moves the estimated effect from -279 to -583 out to -978 to -1,438. Standard SCM on this panel returns -1,297. Lengthening the chain fiftyfold does not disturb this: at 25000/25000 the published specification returns 195.5 and -390, and the linear basis returns 141.3 and -1,123, so the separation holds at the chain length the paper's own convergence discussion would favour. The reported -434 is specific to the constant, and the effect path the linear basis recovers is the one the application would lead a reader to expect: averaged over the seeds it is about -198 in 1990, -1,208 by 1996 and -2,385 by 2003, growing across the window instead of holding flat. The fit does not return all the way to 61, so the constant is not the whole of the gap, but it is most of it.

The B-MV figure is not a one-off run of mine. `mlsynth`'s `MVBBSC` is a clean-room NumPyro port of the Martinez and Vives-i-Bastida generative model, and it is cross-validated against the authors' own `bsynth` package cell by cell on this very panel as a standing benchmark in the library (`benchmarks/cases/mvbbsc_germany.py`, reference script `benchmarks/R/mvbbsc_bsynth_ref.R`, captured against `bsynth` at commit `22d960f`): pre-1990 RMSE 62.14 against 61.96, mean post-1990 ATT -2081.7 against -2064.6, and mean pre-1990 credible-band width 297.1 against 296.6. The reference is `bayesianSynth` with `predictor_match = FALSE`, which is the outcome-only model with no covariates and no Gaussian-process term.

That last detail matters for a comparison the authors might otherwise question. The B-MV fit of 62 is obtained *without* a GP. BASC's 169 is obtained *with* one. If anything the two are stacked in BASC's favour, and it still fits nearly three times worse.

## The reported "standard SCM" weights (Table 7)

A separate problem sits in the paper's Table 7, which reports each method's West Germany donor weights. The "standard SCM" (s-SCM) column is essentially uniform. The weights are roughly 0.04 to 0.05 on every donor, with a single 0.34 spike on Spain. However, the genuine ADH solution is sparse and led by Austria. Those weights are the entire s-SCM model, standard SCM having no other moving part, so its in-sample fit is just their dot product with the donor GDP series, which any reader can check against the authors' own numbers.

I apply this test only to the s-SCM column, and deliberately. BASC and B-MV add a Gaussian-process term to the weighted donor average, so for those two the weights alone do not determine the counterfactual and a dot product would misrepresent the model. For standard SCM there is nothing else to add.

```{python}
#| label: tbl7
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from mlsynth.utils.datautils import dataprep

# Canonical reshape: dataprep returns the treated vector, the donor matrix (aligned
# to donor_names), and the pre/post split
prep = dataprep(d, "country", "year", "gdp", "treat")
y7 = np.asarray(prep["y"]).flatten()
D7 = np.asarray(prep["donor_matrix"])
names7 = list(prep["donor_names"])
pre7 = prep["pre_periods"]

# Table 7 "standard SCM" weights (CSDA-D-25-01439R1, p.31)
s_scm = {"USA": .05, "UK": .05, "Austria": .05, "Belgium": .05, "Denmark": .05, "France": .04,
         "Italy": .04, "Netherlands": .04, "Norway": .05, "Switzerland": .04, "Japan": .04,
         "Greece": .03, "Portugal": .04, "Spain": .34, "Australia": .04, "New Zealand": .05}

def dot_fit(wdict):
    syn = D7 @ np.array([wdict[n] for n in names7])         # synthetic = donor_matrix . weights
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y7[:pre7] - syn[:pre7]) ** 2)))
    att = float(np.mean(y7[pre7:] - syn[pre7:]))
    return round(rmse, 1), round(att, 1)

rmse_s, att_s = dot_fit(s_scm)
rmse_u, att_u = dot_fit({n: 1 / 16 for n in names7})
Markdown(pd.DataFrame({
    "Weight vector": ["s-SCM (Table 7)", "uniform (1/16)", "VanillaSC"],
    "pre-1990 RMSE": [rmse_s, rmse_u, 60.8],
    "post-1990 ATT": [att_s, att_u, -1297.5],
}).to_markdown(index=False))
```

Two things follow, using only the authors' own weights. First, the s-SCM column fits the pre-1990 path at an RMSE near 1,925, against about 1,289 for uniform weights and about 61 for the synthetic control reported above. Standard SCM is defined as the simplex vector minimising pre-treatment squared error, so a vector attaining 1,925 cannot be the solution to that problem when another feasible vector drives the same criterion to 61. The reported column is not a solved standard synthetic control, and no property of my solver is needed to say so. Second, those same weights imply a post-1990 ATT near +2,900, with West Germany above its synthetic, while the paper's text (p.32) reports an s-SCM ATT of -159, the opposite sign. The Table 7 s-SCM column and the reported s-SCM effect cannot both come from the same estimator, and I would like an explanation of why.

The table prints weights to two decimals, so it is fair to ask whether that rounding is doing the damage. It is not. Perturbing the sixteen weights independently within the full printing error and renormalising to the simplex, over 4,000 draws, moves the pre-1990 RMSE only within 1,861 to 2,002 and leaves the implied ATT positive in every draw (2,731 to 3,088). The conclusion does not depend on the printed precision.

```{python}
#| label: tbl7-rounding
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
w0 = np.array([s_scm[n] for n in names7])
_r, _a = [], []
for _ in range(4000):
    wp = np.clip(w0 + rng.uniform(-0.005, 0.005, size=w0.size), 0, None)
    wp = wp / wp.sum()
    syn = D7 @ wp
    _r.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((y7[:pre7] - syn[:pre7]) ** 2)))
    _a.append(np.mean(y7[pre7:] - syn[pre7:]))
Markdown(pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["pre-1990 RMSE", "post-1990 ATT"],
    "as printed": [rmse_s, att_s],
    "min over rounding": [round(min(_r), 1), round(min(_a), 1)],
    "max over rounding": [round(max(_r), 1), round(max(_a), 1)],
}).to_markdown(index=False))
```

Drawn on the same axes, a correctly solved standard SCM (`VanillaSC`) and the Bayesian SCM the paper builds on (`MVBBSC`) are indistinguishable from observed West Germany through the pre-1990 window, while the counterfactual implied by the Table 7 s-SCM weights sits well below it the entire time.

```{python}
#| label: fig-three-scm
#| fig-cap: "West Germany: observed versus a correctly solved standard SCM (VanillaSC), the Bayesian SCM the paper builds on (mlsynth's MVBBSC), and the counterfactual implied by the paper's own Table 7 s-SCM weights. The two correctly computed fits are indistinguishable from observed West Germany across the pre-1990 window (shaded); the Table 7 weights sit below it the entire pre-period, so their implied post-1990 effect comes out positive, the wrong sign."
def _curve(label):
    s = cmp.curves[cmp.curves["method"] == label].sort_values("period")
    return s["period"].to_numpy(dtype=float), s["counterfactual"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

yr_v, cf_vsc = _curve("VanillaSC (outcome-only)")
yr_m, cf_mvb = _curve("B-MV (MVBBSC, mlsynth)")
cf_t7 = D7 @ np.array([s_scm[n] for n in names7])          # Table 7 weights . donor matrix

wg  = d[d.country == "West Germany"].sort_values("year")
yrs = wg["year"].to_numpy(dtype=float); obs = wg["gdp"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
_pre = yrs < 1990
_rmse = lambda cf: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((obs[_pre] - cf[_pre]) ** 2)))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.axvspan(yrs.min(), 1990, color="0.92", zorder=0)
ax.axvline(1990, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.plot(yrs,  obs,    color="black",   lw=2.6, label="West Germany (observed)", zorder=6)
ax.plot(yr_v, cf_vsc, color="#1f77b4", lw=2.0, label=f"Standard SCM (VanillaSC), pre-RMSE {_rmse(cf_vsc):.0f}", zorder=5)
ax.plot(yr_m, cf_mvb, color="#2ca02c", lw=2.0, label=f"B-MV (mlsynth MVBBSC), pre-RMSE {_rmse(cf_mvb):.0f}", zorder=5)
ax.plot(yrs,  cf_t7,  color="#d62728", lw=2.2, ls="--", label=f"Table 7 s-SCM weights, pre-RMSE {_rmse(cf_t7):.0f}", zorder=4)
ax.set_title("West Germany: observed vs. three standard-SCM counterfactuals")
ax.set_xlabel("year"); ax.set_ylabel("GDP per capita")
ax.set_xlim(yrs.min(), yrs.max())
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## The reported effects do not sit together


The paper's five ATT estimates (p.32) are -434 for BASC, -218 for B-MV, -159 for standard SCM, -1,655 for fPCA-SYNTH and -2,427 for ClusterSC, all described as per-capita units. Set them beside what the same methods return on the same panel:

| Method (paper's label) | Paper's ATT (p.32) | Reproduced here | Reproduced pre-1990 RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|
| BASC | -434 | -390 to -702 (authors' own sampler) | 169-195 |
| fPCA-SYNTH (Bayani 2021) | -1,655 | -1,501 (`CLUSTERSC`, RPCA-SC) | 88.6 |
| ClusterSC (Rho et al. 2025) | -2,427 | -2,039 (`CLUSTERSC`, PCR/RSC) | 98.0 |
| B-MV | -218 | -2,075 (`bsynth`) / -2,079 (`MVBBSC`) | 62.2 / 62.1 |
| standard SCM | -159 | -1,298 (`VanillaSC`) | 60.8 |

Three of the five reproduce. BASC does, as noted above. fPCA-SYNTH is the functional-PCA screen followed by robust PCA and non-negative least squares set out in Section 2.4.1; `CLUSTERSC`'s RPCA-SC path is that procedure, and it returns -1,501 against the reported -1,655, about nine percent apart. ClusterSC is the SVD-clustering-plus-PCR procedure of Rho et al.; `CLUSTERSC`'s PCR/RSC path returns -2,039 against the reported -2,427, about sixteen percent. Both are within the range I would expect two runs of a two-stage screen to differ by, and I raise no objection to either as an effect estimate.

The fPCA-SYNTH row does carry a smaller question, because Section 5 states that it "is implemented using the `mlsynth` package in Python", which is the package I am running. Two runs of the same code should agree exactly, so the nine percent needs a source. Section 5 gives the two settings: the number of functional principal components chosen by the elbow rule to explain at least 90% of pre-intervention variation, and the number of clusters chosen by maximising the average silhouette coefficient. Running `CLUSTERSC` that way returns -1,500.9, and the variance target does not move it: 0.90 through 0.95 all select the same components and return the same estimate. Fixing the cluster count by hand moves it as far as -1,620.0 at four or five clusters, which the silhouette criterion does not select here. So the reported -1,655 is not recovered at the stated settings. A version difference is the most likely explanation, since the package has changed since the analysis was run, and I raise it only because the replication script would settle in one line what I can otherwise only guess at.

That is what isolates the last two rows. The paper is working on a scale where an effect of -1,655 or -2,427 is the natural size, because three of its own five numbers are, and I can obtain all three. Standard SCM and B-MV are reported an order of magnitude below what those methods return on the same panel, so a single mis-scaled outcome does not account for it: whatever produced -218 and -159 was applied to those two methods and not to the other three. They are also the two whose reported values I can check most directly, standard SCM through the weight vector Table 7 prints in full and B-MV because two independent implementations of it exist.

The BASC row carries a caveat in the authors' favour. My chains are far shorter than theirs: 500/500, 2,000/2,000 and 25,000/25,000 against the paper's three chains of 500,000 after 500,000 burn-in, which Section 5 reports as converged with Gelman-Rubin below 1.01 and diagnoses further in Appendix C.2. Across my three the ATT moves over -702, -583 and -390 without settling, so I do not read the gap from the reported -434 as a discrepancy. It is most likely my burn-in, and the reported value has the better claim to being the converged one.

What matters for this report is that the in-sample fit is not similarly unstable. It stays in a 169 to 195 band across a fiftyfold change in chain length, and the shortest and longest chains bracket the same conclusion. The fit finding does not depend on chain length; the ATT reproduction does, and I am not resting anything on it.

The direction is also one-sided. At -159 and -218, BASC's -434 sits unremarkably among its comparators, larger than the two classical benchmarks and smaller than the two robust ones. At the values those methods actually return, -1,298 and -2,079, BASC is the smallest estimate in the table by a factor of three, and the ordering that supports the paper's competitiveness claim on this application does not survive. I make no claim about how this arose. I do think it has to be resolved before the West Germany application can be read as evidence for the method.

This section carries less weight than its length suggests. It is the part of my report the authors are most likely to answer, and answering it would not settle the review. Suppose every reported ATT is confirmed as computed on the raw per-capita series exactly as stated, and the -218 and -159 turn out to be correct for whatever was actually run. The two findings that motivate this report are untouched. The donor weights are still estimated from the post-treatment outcomes, which is a property of Equation (7) and of the sampler that fits it, and the weight vector printed in Table 7 still fits the pre-1990 path worse than uniform weights do. Neither is an inference from the reported ATTs. The first is read off the model, confirmed by running the authors' own sampler, and reproduced by least squares from their published weights; the second uses nothing but their published numbers.

```{python}
#| label: fig-paths
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
cmp.plot(ax=ax)                                   # mlsynth methods + observed
ax.plot(basc_cf["year"], basc_cf["synthetic"], color="#d62728", lw=2.2,
        label="BASC", zorder=5)
ax.axvspan(basc_cf["year"].min(), 1990, color="0.92", zorder=0)
ax.axvline(1990, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_title("West Germany: observed vs synthetic counterfactuals")
ax.set_xlabel("year"); ax.set_ylabel("GDP per capita")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

BASC's own posterior path, with its 95% credible band, is below. The band raises a second issue on its own account, separately from the fit.

```{python}
#| label: basc-coverage
_pre = basc_cf[basc_cf["year"] < 1990]
_in = ((_pre["observed"] >= _pre["lo95"]) & (_pre["observed"] <= _pre["hi95"]))
Markdown(
    f"In the pre-treatment period the 95% credible band contains the observed West "
    f"German series in {int(_in.sum())} of {len(_pre)} years, with a mean band "
    f"width of {float((_pre['hi95'] - _pre['lo95']).mean()):.0f} per-capita units."
)
```

I raise this as a question about what the band represents, not as a coverage failure. A posterior credible band for a latent counterfactual mean is not an object one should expect to contain a noisy observed series 95% of the time, and the gap between the two depends on whether the reported interval is for the latent mean, for the posterior predictive, or for the counterfactual trajectory inclusive of the error term. The paper does not say which. What can be said without settling that is that the band is narrow, with a mean pre-treatment width about the size of the pre-treatment RMSE itself, and that it excludes the observed series in two thirds of the years where that series is observed. The authors should state which quantity the reported band is an interval for, and explain why the observed pre-treatment trajectory falls outside it in twenty of thirty years.

```{python}
#| label: fig-basc-ci
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.axvspan(basc_cf["year"].min(), 1990, color="0.92", zorder=0)
ax.fill_between(basc_cf["year"], basc_cf["lo95"], basc_cf["hi95"], color="#d62728", alpha=0.15, label="BASC 95% CI")
ax.plot(basc_cf["year"], basc_cf["synthetic"], color="#d62728", lw=2, label="BASC synthetic")
ax.plot(basc_cf["year"], basc_cf["observed"], color="black", lw=2.4, label="West Germany (observed)")
ax.axvline(1990, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("year"); ax.set_ylabel("GDP per capita")
ax.set_title("BASC posterior counterfactual (2000/2000)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Bottom line

For us to continue reviewing this, the authors' GitHub page needs everything that went into producing these results, not their BASC code alone: data import, cleaning, the runs of fPCA-SC and ClusterSC, the code for B-MV, and the solver that produced the s-SCM weight vector in Table 7. Every reported effect also needs its in-sample RMSE beside it, so the claims can be checked against the syntax that produced them.

This request is narrower than it may sound, because the repository as it stands supplies exactly one of the five methods in Table 7. `github.com/sll-lee/paper-BASC` contains `BASC_realdata.R` and the `repgermany` data, and that script runs the BASC sampler and nothing else. There is no code in it for standard SCM, B-MV, fPCA-SYNTH or ClusterSC. `tidysynth` is declared in the script's package list and never called anywhere in the file, which is the only trace of a comparison method in the repository.

The full script is the one non-negotiable item, and it is a larger request than the West Germany section on its own would justify. The argument for it is four steps.

Two of the four comparison methods I could independently check reproduce the paper: fPCA-SYNTH to nine percent and ClusterSC to sixteen. Two produce materially different results from those reported: standard SCM and B-MV, each an order of magnitude away. Those two are the textbook estimator and the Bayesian synthetic control BASC is built on. And one of them, standard SCM, fails an elementary check on the paper's own published weights, with no implementation of mine involved.

The same four methods appear throughout the numerical study, on which the competitiveness claim now rests alone. Whatever routine produced the Table 7 s-SCM column is presumably the routine that produced standard SCM in every simulation cell in Tables 3 to 6, and no reader can determine whether it is mis-specified there too. Only the complete pipeline, from data import through cleaning, solver specification and reporting, can establish where the discrepancies originate.

Two smaller points on the repository, offered as housekeeping. The README's structure block names `BASC_basc_realdata.R` and its run instructions say `source("clean_basc_realdata.R")`, while the file that is actually present is `BASC_realdata.R`; neither of the documented names exists. And the README says the data file may be absent for licensing reasons, but `data/repgermany.dta` is in fact committed.

In-sample fit is not the sole determining factor in the validity of a novel SCM, and the comparison table shows why: Amjad's Robust SC and Bayani's Robust PCA SC give up a little fit against the ADH 2015 baseline and buy something for it, namely results as good as the original without matching on predictors. That trade is a defensible one. BASC's is a different case. It is not slightly worse than the baseline toolkit, it is three times worse than the model it nests, and it does not compete with Forward DID, a uniformly weighted subset of controls plus an intercept. The paper claims competitiveness in the simulation studies; on the canonical dataset it has not been demonstrated.

## Recommendation

Major revision.

Three things are not in question. The Gamma-Bernoulli construction that places posterior mass on simplex faces is a genuine contribution, Theorem 3.3 is correct as proved, and I raise no objection to the design of the numerical study. Nothing above establishes that the method is unsound, and I would not want the paper rejected.

Most of my concerns sit in Section 5, in Table 7, and in what a referee can verify. One does not. That the donor weights are estimated over the full sample is a property of Equation (7), not of this application, and the same specification generates every cell of the numerical study, so it has to be answered on its merits and not by correcting the West Germany section. Theorem 3.3 does not answer it, because the model it is proved on excludes the term that causes it. The following would resolve the set.


1. The full replication script, for everything, as set out above. This is the condition the rest depend on: several of the items below cannot be assessed by a referee until the code exists.

2. Rerun Section 5 with a non-constant effect basis, and report Table 7 and the ATT under it. Because Equation (7) is fitted over all 44 years while $q = 1$ gives the post-treatment term a single constant, the donor weights absorb the part of the widening post-1990 gap that the constant cannot represent. In the authors' own sampler, adding the $D_{2t} = t - T_0$ term that Section 3.1 already describes moves the pre-1990 fit from 166 to 222 down to 135 to 149 and the effect from -279 to -583 out to -978 to -1,438, against -1,297 for standard SCM. This is the finding I would most want addressed, and the remedy is inside the paper's existing framework. If the constant is preferred on other grounds, the paper needs to argue that the weights remain interpretable when they are fitted partly to the effect being estimated, and the reported -434 needs to be presented as conditional on that choice.

3. Recompute Table 7 and reconcile it with the text. The reported s-SCM weight vector fits the pre-1990 path worse than uniform weights and implies a post-1990 effect of the opposite sign to the s-SCM effect reported on p.32. It cannot be the solution to the standard synthetic-control problem, and the table and text cannot both be right.

4. Reconcile the reported standard SCM and B-MV effects. Both are reported an order of magnitude below what those methods return on this panel, while fPCA-SYNTH and ClusterSC are not.

5. Report in-sample fit alongside every reported effect, for every method, in the application and in the simulations. Pre-treatment fit is the diagnostic by which synthetic control estimates are conventionally judged, and its absence is why the discrepancies above survived a round of review.

6. Report convergence diagnostics for the real-data fit specifically, and state which quantity the reported credible band is an interval for. The band contains the observed series in ten of thirty pre-treatment years, and what that indicates depends on whether the interval is for the latent mean, the posterior predictive, or the counterfactual trajectory inclusive of the error term.

Items 2, 3 and 4 are the ones I would want resolved before the paper is reconsidered, and item 2 is the one that reaches past this application. Item 1 is what makes any of it checkable.


## Reproducibility: the offline benchmarks

The toolkit rows run at render time. The BASC 500/500 and 2000/2000 rows and the B-MV row are regenerated at render time from saved posterior counterfactuals. The BASC 25000/25000 row is a single long offline chain, and both of its summary numbers are now read from `data/gamma1_diagnostic.csv`, which `scripts/run_gamma1.R` writes: its control configuration is the authors' sampler with the patch inactive, and it returns in-sample RMSE 195.516 and post-1990 ATT -389.799, the values this report previously carried as literals. The scripts and data behind the offline pieces are given below so each can be reproduced against a known state of this repository.

```{python}
#| label: stamp
#| echo: false
import subprocess
def _git(*a):
    try:
        return subprocess.run(["git", *a], capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=ROOT).stdout.strip() or "unknown"
    except Exception:
        return "unknown"
Markdown(f"Reproduced against `mlsynth` at commit `{_git('rev-parse', '--short', 'HEAD')}` "
         f"({_git('log', '-1', '--format=%ci')}).")
```

The chain uses the authors' own sampler (`safe_chol` ... `run_basc_chain` from
`github.com/sll-lee/paper-BASC`, sourced as `basc_funcs.R`) on the West Germany
outcome and 16-donor matrix exported from `basedata/repgermany.dta`. It is
identical to `scripts/basc_run.R` except for the chain length, and is shown here,
not executed.

```r
# BASC on West Germany, 25000 burn-in + 25000 sampling (single chain, seed 200).
#   -> in-sample (pre-1990) RMSE = 195.516,  post-1990 ATT = -389.799
suppressMessages(library(MASS))
rinvgamma <- function(n, shape, scale) 1 / rgamma(n, shape = shape, rate = scale)
rtmvnorm <- function(n, mean, sigma, upper, ...) {   # q=1, diagonal, upper-truncated
  sdv <- sqrt(diag(as.matrix(sigma))); qd <- length(mean); out <- numeric(qd)
  for (i in seq_len(qd)) {
    p <- pnorm((upper[i] - mean[i]) / sdv[i])
    out[i] <- mean[i] + sdv[i] * qnorm(runif(1, 0, max(p, 1e-12)))
  }
  matrix(out, nrow = 1)
}
rdist <- function(x1, x2 = NULL) {
  x1 <- as.matrix(x1); if (is.null(x2)) x2 <- x1 else x2 <- as.matrix(x2)
  outer(seq_len(nrow(x1)), seq_len(nrow(x2)),
        Vectorize(function(i, j) sqrt(sum((x1[i, ] - x2[j, ])^2))))
}
source("basc_funcs.R")                        # authors' safe_chol .. run_basc_chain

y  <- as.numeric(read.csv("y.csv", header = FALSE)[, 1])    # West Germany GDP (44)
x  <- as.matrix(read.csv("x.csv", header = FALSE))          # 16 donors x 44 years
vt <- seq_len(length(y)); Dt <- as.integer(vt >= 31)        # treatment from 1990
j <- ncol(x); t <- length(vt); N <- 25000; nburn <- 25000   # (paper uses 500000/500000)

chain <- run_basc_chain(seed = 200, y = y, x = x, vt = vt, Dt = Dt, N = N, nburn = nburn, q = 1)

g <- chain$gamma.sample; u <- chain$u.sample
beta <- matrix(0, N, j); for (i in 1:N) beta[i, ] <- (g[i, ] * u[i, ]) / sum(g[i, ] * u[i, ])
y.samp <- matrix(0, N, t)
for (i in 1:N) y.samp[i, ] <- as.numeric(x %*% beta[i, ] + chain$f.sample[i, ])
cf <- colMeans(y.samp); pre <- vt < 31; post <- vt >= 31
cat(sprintf("in-sample RMSE = %.3f   post-1990 ATT = %.3f\n",
            sqrt(mean((y[pre] - cf[pre])^2)), mean(y[post] - cf[post])))
```

The B-MV counterfactual (`data/bmv_counterfactual.csv`) is the Martinez and
Vives-i-Bastida (2024) Bayesian SCM computed with the authors' cited `bsynth`
package (Ignacio Martinez's implementation, `github.com/ignacio82/bsynth`), built
from source and run as

```r
bayesianSynth$new(data = repgermany, time = year, id = country, treated = D,
                  outcome = gdp, ci_width = 0.95, predictor_match = FALSE)$fit(cores = 4)
```

on the `repgermany` panel (`D = 1` for West Germany from 1990), the same
outcome-only configuration as bsynth's own West Germany example. `predictor_match
= FALSE` selects `bsynth`'s model 1: no covariates and no Gaussian-process term.
Its posterior-mean counterfactual gives pre-1990 RMSE 62.2 and post-1990 ATT -2075.

This is also a standing cross-validation in `mlsynth`, not a one-off run made
for this report. `benchmarks/cases/mvbbsc_germany.py` pins `MVBBSC` against
`bsynth` on this panel cell by cell, with the reference script committed at
`benchmarks/R/mvbbsc_bsynth_ref.R` and the captured output under
`benchmarks/reference/mvbbsc_germany/` (against `bsynth` at commit `22d960f`):

| quantity | `MVBBSC` | `bsynth` |
|---|---|---|
| pre-1990 RMSE | 62.14 | 61.96 |
| mean post-1990 ATT | -2081.7 | -2064.6 |
| mean pre-1990 band width | 297.1 | 296.6 |
| mean post-1990 band width | 1123.3 | 1143.2 |
